L634@P24: The HRT can strengthen its approach to using outcomes for
L635@P24: measuring progress toward goals and keeping the public
L636@P24: informed.
L637@P24: The three goals guiding the HRT’s work in encampments were to reduce unsheltered homelessness, mitigate
L638@P24: dangerous encampments, and maintain a clean City. The HRT tracked some outcomes related to these program
L639@P24: goals during the audit period but reported information cumulatively which made it difficult to identify trends
L640@P24: over time. They also did not report on other outcomes that could connect to their goal of reducing unsheltered
L641@P24: homelessness, though they expanded on reported outcomes in a May 2025 report to Council. Going forward, it
L642@P24: will be important for the HRT to consistently report on these outcomes related to their goals. Additionally, the
L643@P24: HRT could improve the accessibility of their public reporting. Limited administrative staffing may constrain the
L644@P24: HRT’s ability to collect, measure and report data, though it is important to fill gaps where possible.
L645@P24: Reporting on more outcomes with consistency could help connect the HRT’s work
L646@P24: with their goals, but additional resources may be needed.
L647@P24: The HRT tracked some outcomes related to their program goals during the audit period. The
L648@P24: three goals guiding their work in encampments were: our residents are sheltered, dangerous encampments are
L649@P24: not inevitable, and our City is clean. To assess progress towards those goals, the HRT tracked the outcomes
L650@P24-25: listed in the table below (Figure 14).Homeless Response Team: Opportunities Exist to Strengthen Procedures and Better Track Outcomes

L679@P25: Reporting information by standardized reporting periods rather than cumulatively can make it
L680@P25: easier to assess HRT’s progress toward its goals. During the audit period, the HRT reported on
L681@P25: outcomes in their quarterly reports to Council as cumulative numbers, for example, 59 encampments closures
L682@P25: or 655 shelter offers between 2021 and 2024 (Figure 14). Reporting this information as a total over the duration
L683@P25: of the program, rather than by standard reporting periods such as per quarter, made it difficult to evaluate
L684@P25: progress toward the HRT’s goals or identify trends over time.
L685@P25: While the HRT reported on the outcomes above during the audit period, they did not report on
L686@P25: other outcomes that could be useful to connect to the goal reducing unsheltered homelessness.
L687@P25: For example, USICH recommends reporting on outreach outcomes like number of Coordinated Entry
L688@P25: assessments or number of outreach encounters, which can shed light on the starting point of the process to get
L689@P25: people connected to services and sheltered. Additionally, while the HRT reported the number of shelter offers
L690@P25: and acceptances, they did not report on the number of actual shelter enrollments. This information is important
L691@P25: because according to a sample of internal HRT data, people who accept shelter may not end up enrolling in
L692@P25: shelter. Reporting on enrollment could help provide insight into challenges unhoused residents face to getting
L693@P25: into shelter. Another city that reports shelter enrollment information is Seattle, which reports not only the
L694@P25: number of shelter offers made and the number of accepted offers, but also reports the number of people who
L695@P25-26: enrolled in shelter. Homeless Response Team: Opportunities Exist to Strengthen Procedures and Better Track Outcomes
L696@P26: 27
L697@P26: Additionally, the HRT did not report on the reasons why people declined shelter offers during
L698@P26: the audit period. Reporting on reasons that people decline shelter offers can better demonstrate success or
L699@P26: reveal barriers in connecting encampment residents to shelter. People decline shelter enrollment for many
L700@P26: reasons. As an example, the HRT has stated they generally see a higher shelter acceptance rate with noncongregate beds instead of congregate beds. Although there are challenges to systematically collecting this data,
L701@P26: even limited or anecdotal data on why people decline shelter offers could provide additional insight into barriers
L702@P26: to getting people sheltered. Additionally, the City requires Bay Area Community Services (BACS) – one of its
L703@P26: contracted service providers – to collect data on why the people they engaged with declined shelter offers.
L704@P26: The HRT added new outcomes to its reports to Council in May 2025. Though outside the scope of our
L705@P26: audit, an off-agenda memo the HRT sent to Council on May 12, 2025 reported several additional outcomes
L706@P26: including the number of people who enrolled in shelter and the number of Coordinated Entry assessments. The
L707@P26: memo states that these additional outcomes were intended to provide valuable information to assess progress
L708@P26: towards the first goal to resolve unsheltered homelessness. Going forward, it will be important for the HRT to
L709@P26: consistently report on these outcomes to provide more information on the process of initial outreach to
L710@P26: ultimately being sheltered. This information can help the public and City decision-makers to see trends over
L711@P26: time, understand the connection between the City’s activities and goal of getting people sheltered, and reveal
L712@P26: barriers or gaps that the City should address.
L713@P26: Other useful information to report consistently in all reports to City Council going forward is
L714@P26: demographic data such as race, gender, and health conditions for encampment residents.
L715@P26: Continuing to report on demographics where possible, such as race, gender and disability status, can help
L716@P26: identify barriers to providing and care. For instance, disability status may affect someone’s ability to accept a
L717@P26: shelter offer if it is not ADA-compliant. Similarly, someone may hesitate to accept an offer of shelter for fear of
L718@P26: experiencing gender-based violence. Advocates who work with the unsheltered population in Berkeley have
L719@P26: explained that understanding the characteristics and needs of this population provides important context when
L720@P26: planning encampment actions.18 As one advocate stated:
L721@P26: For people with physical or mental disabilities – these shortcomings become overwhelming. It doesn’t
L722@P26: take much to make a mistake that can jettison the efforts an individual has put forth. Many people in
L723@P26: encampments, older folks, a lot of people are out there with serious handicaps, and we don’t really
L724@P26: approach that… I’ve been running into people in their 60s and 70s, and they are not going to be
L725@P26: gainfully employed. We need to take these things into consideration.
L726@P26-27: 18 Some of the points raised by advocates may be subject to litigation and this audit did not independently investigate all their claims. Homeless Response Team: Opportunities Exist to Strengthen Procedures and Better Track Outcomes
L727@P27: 28
L728@P27: Consistent reporting on this information is especially important given that the May 2025 memo pointed out that
L729@P27: HRT participants are far more vulnerable than Alameda County’s homeless population overall. For example, the
L730@P27: memo stated that a larger proportion of HRT participants reported physical disabilities, mental health
L731@P27: disorders, or substance use disorders compared to the overall homeless population in Alameda County.
L732@P27: Reporting on this information can also help track HRT’s progress in serving these residents and inform
L733@P27: allocation of resources to effectively provide services.
L734@P27: There are some challenges to consistently collecting data and reporting on outcomes. The HRT
L735@P27: stated that their reporting is an evolving and imperfect practice because there are few industry tools for
L736@P27: measuring encampment outcomes and they have adapted their reporting over time based on what has worked
L737@P27: for them. Additionally, some data may be difficult to systematically track and measure. For example, HMIS does
L738@P27: not have a data field for reasons why people decline shelter, making this metric difficult to quantify.
L739@P27: Additional resources may be needed to consistently measure and report on outcomes. HRT staff
L740@P27: explained they had limited budget and administrative support for data analysis and reporting. A 2024 staffing
L741@P27: study of the Neighborhood Services Division found that some staff felt overburdened by administrative
L742@P27: responsibilities. Although the study recommended hiring an additional administrative support staff position,
L743@P27: the division did not receive funding for it. Without robust data collection, analysis, and reporting, it may be
L744@P27: difficult to identify outreach gaps, track results, or for City leadership to make strategic decisions and allocate
L745@P27: resources effectively.
L746@P27: The HRT's reports were difficult to access on the City’s website.
L747@P27: Over the audit period, the HRT’s public reports were not easily accessible. The HRT’s reports were published in
L748@P27: two different places on the City’s website without a central landing page, which made it difficult to access
L749@P27: information about the HRT's work in encampments. As a comparison, other jurisdictions provide the public
L750@P27: with more accessible information on their efforts to assist encampment residents. We did not assess staff
L751@P27: resources in benchmark jurisdictions compared to Berkeley; these are examples of public reporting methods
L752@P27: that may be useful for Berkeley to consider, keeping in mind resource constraints.
L753@P27: The City and County of San Francisco makes information about coordinated entry accessible to the public
L754@P27-28: (Figure 15). Homeless Response Team: Opportunities Exist to Strengthen Procedures and Better Track Outcomes

L759@P28: Additionally, a few jurisdictions we reviewed also provided information related to outreach efforts on their
L760@P28: online dashboard (Figures 16-17). For example, the City of Issaquah reports on the number of monthly face-toface interactions with clients. The City of Portland shows the number helped into shelter and the number given
L761@P28: housing referrals, among other outcomes.

L769@P29: Comprehensive and accessible public reporting aligns with best practices. For example, USICH recommends
L770@P29: developing a public-facing dashboard to show progress on reducing unsheltered homelessness and encampment
L771@P29: resolution strategies. In 2022, the HRT worked on a dashboard that included data such as shelter enrollments,
L772@P29: program exits and exit destinations. However, the team put the project on hold, though they stated they are
L773@P29: interested in producing a dashboard in the future.
L774@P29: Not being able to easily access HRT data on a website or dashboard means that Council and members of the
L775@P29: public may not understand the extent to which the HRT has been successful in achieving program goals of
L776@P29: reducing unsheltered homelessness. It also becomes difficult for oversight bodies, such as the Homeless
L777@P29: Services Panel of Experts, to provide adequate oversight over the HRT’s activities if they are not able to access
L778@P29: information.19
L779@P29: Recommendations
L780@P29: To more effectively measure the impact of their work and enhance transparency, the HRT should:
L781@P29: 3.1 Expand reported outcomes that align with the HRT’s goals and define how they will be measured.
L782@P29: Public reporting could include key information such as outreach efforts and shelter enrollments,
L783@P29: along with demographic breakdowns and reasons people decline shelter, where possible. Report on
L784@P29: the same outcomes over time using a consistent timeframe to support comparisons.
L785@P29: 19 The Homeless Services Panel of Experts (HSPE) was established with Measure P in 2018 to make recommendations on the City’s
L786@P29-30: funding for programs to end or prevent homelessness in Berkeley and provide humane services and support. Homeless Response Team: Opportunities Exist to Strengthen Procedures and Better Track Outcomes
L787@P30: 31
L788@P30: To improve the accessibility of public reporting, the HRT should:
L789@P30: 3.2 Consider sharing public data in a more accessible format, such as on a single landing page on the
L790@P30: City’s website or through a dashboard.
L791@P30: To ensure there is adequate staffing to focus on reporting and the measurement of impact, the City
L792@P30: Manager’s Office should:
L793@P30: 3.3 Assess staffing resources needed to support data and reporting efforts without impacting HRT’s
L794@P30-31: operational duties. Homeless Response Team: Opportunities Exist to Strengthen Procedures and Better Track Outcomes

L796@P31: Recommendations and Management Response
L797@P31: We provided a draft of this report to the HRT and city management for review and comment. City management
L798@P31: agreed with our findings, conclusions, and recommendations. We generally expect the City to implement audit
L799@P31: recommendations within two years of report issuance. The department provided the implementation dates and
L800@P31: corrective action plan below. We will be conducting our standard recommendation follow-up process after the
L801@P31: audit is issued. We have not yet confirmed to what extent the recommendations have been implemented prior to
L802@P31: the audit release date.
L803@P31: 2.1 Document the coordination structure for encampment-related meetings. Continue to meet regularly
L804@P31: with key participants as identified by the City for all encampment outreach and interventions.

L927@P35: Methodology and Statement of Compliance
L928@P35: We audited the Homeless Response Team’s (HRT) operations for fiscal years (FY) 2022 through 2024. We
L929@P35: performed a risk assessment of the HRT’s practices and procedures to identify potential internal control
L930@P35: weaknesses, including fraud risks, within the context of our audit objectives. This included a review of selected
L931@P35: policies and procedures, as well as interviews with internal staff.
L932@P35: To gain an understanding of the HRT’s operations and internal controls and to achieve our audit objectives, we
L933@P35: used the following methodology:
L934@P35:  We reviewed internal policies and procedures, meeting notes, email communications, and other
L935@P35: documentation related to HRT operations, interagency coordination, and encampment response
L936@P35: efforts.
L937@P35:  We analyzed HRT data related to encampment activities, service connections, and outreach outcomes.
L938@P35: We evaluated the quality and consistency of data collection practices and assessed how the HRT used
L939@P35: data to measure progress toward its goals. We also reviewed how outcomes were reported to the
L940@P35: public, including through City Council materials, performance reports, and public communications.
L941@P35: We evaluated the clarity, completeness, and accessibility of HRT’s public reporting against best
L942@P35: practices in transparency and accountability. While we were unable to verify the accuracy of the HRT’s
L943@P35: internal data, we analyzed their data reporting in our audit in order to understand how they
L944@P35: communicate information to the public and make recommendations for improvement.
L945@P35:  We compared HRT practices against published best practices and guidance from organizations such as
L946@P35: the U.S. Interagency Council on Homelessness (USICH), as well as models used in other jurisdictions
L947@P35: with similar encampment response challenges.
L948@P35:  We reviewed documents and sources that shaped the operating context for the HRT, including:
L949@P35: o Biennial city budgets to understand HRT funding and staffing resources.
L950@P35: o Berkeley Municipal Code and Administrative Regulations related to encampments,
L951@P35: homelessness response, and interdepartmental coordination.
L952@P35: o Local and federal court cases that influenced encampment policy, including Prado v.
L953@P35: City of Berkeley, Johnson v. Grants Pass, and Martin v. Boise.
L954@P35: o City Council materials and reports that documented policy decisions and legal
L955@P35-36: considerations relevant to HRT operations. Homeless Response Team: Opportunities Exist to Strengthen Procedures and Better Track Outcomes
L956@P36: 37
L957@P36:  We interviewed a wide range of stakeholders to understand how the HRT coordinates with others and
L958@P36: uses data in its work. This included HRT staff and staff from other city departments involved in
L959@P36: homelessness response, Alameda County officials, and contracted outreach and service providers. We
L960@P36: also spoke with members of the Homeless Services Panel of Experts, city leadership, and homeless
L961@P36: advocates. These interviews provided insight into coordination challenges, service delivery gaps, and
L962@P36: differing perspectives on the City’s approach to encampments.
L963@P36:  We attended community meetings held by city leadership regarding homeless encampment response
L964@P36: to better understand how information was shared with the public and how community concerns and
L965@P36: feedback were addressed. These meetings provided additional context for assessing the City’s
L966@P36: communication practices and stakeholder engagement.
L967@P36: Data Reliability
L968@P36: We assessed the reliability of encampment data by interviewing data system managers and owners and
L969@P36: examining the data for completeness, consistency, and appropriateness. We determined that the data are
L970@P36: sufficiently reliable for the purposes of our audit.
L971@P36: Though we found the encampment data to be inconsistent and incomplete, we used encampment data to
L972@P36: understand the type of data HRT collects and the data they present to the public, and therefore any
L973@P36: inconsistencies in the data did not affect our audit findings. When cross-checking the data to additional
L974@P36: sources, we could not independently verify certain data fields including the number offered and accepted
L975@P36: shelter, the number of tents or structures, and the number of notices given. Therefore, we did not use the data
L976@P36: for analysis or measurement. Our audit includes recommendations for improving management of encampment
L977@P36: data to increase data system reliability.
L978@P36: Statement of Compliance
L979@P36: We conducted this performance audit in accordance with Generally Accepted Government Auditing Standards.
L980@P36: Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain sufficient, appropriate evidence to
L981@P36: provide a reasonable basis for our findings and conclusions based on our audit objectives. We believe that the
L982@P36-37: evidence obtained provides a reasonable basis for our findings and conclusions based on our audit objectives. Mission Statement
L983@P37: Promoting transparency and accountability in Berkeley government.

L1002@P38: July 29, 2025
L1003@P38: To: Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council

L1006@P38: Track Outcomes
L1007@P38: RECOMMENDATION
L1008@P38: We recommend City Council request that the City Manager report back during the audit followup period in Fall 2026, and annually thereafter, regarding the status of our audit
L1009@P38: recommendations until reported fully implemented by the Homelessness Response Team and
L1010@P38: the City Manager’s Office. The audit includes six recommendations to improve coordination with
L1011@P38: service providers, strengthen data procedures, expand and standardize outcome reporting,
L1012@P38: enhance public transparency, and assess staffing resources needed to support these efforts. The
L1013@P38: City Manager’s Office agreed to our findings and recommendations. Please see our report for
L1014@P38: their complete response.
L1015@P38: FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
L1016@P38: Implementing the audit recommendations will help the City better measure the impact of the
L1017@P38: Homeless Response Team’s work and enhance transparency around the use of public resources.
L1018@P38: Improving coordination with service providers, as recommended in the audit, may require
L1019@P38: continued staff time to maintain regular meetings and implement shared tools like the HMIS
L1020@P38: Outreach module. The HRT stated that limited administrative resources constrained their ability
L1021@P38: to support data and reporting efforts, and a 2024 staffing study recommended additional
L1022@P38: administrative support, though funding was not provided. Additional resources may be needed
L1023@P38: to sustain improvements to coordination, data sharing, and public reporting.
L1024@P38: CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
L1025@P38: The Homeless Response Team (HRT) is an interdepartmental team that conducts both outreach
L1026@P38: and enforcement at encampments in Berkeley. To help move encampment residents indoors,
L1027@P38: the HRT must navigate a complex regional system with limited shelter and housing resources,
L1028@P38: most of which are managed by the Alameda County Continuum of Care. According to the PointIn-Time Count and Berkeley shelter data from the audit period, there were more than twice as
L1029@P38: many people experiencing homelessness as there were shelter beds in Berkeley.
L1030@P38: The HRT paused some coordination meetings with service providers for over a year, which one
L1031@P38: provider said resulted in clients being lost after encampment actions. Although the meetings
L1032@P38: have resumed, the team did not have written procedures for ongoing communication or formal
L1033@P38: coordination structures. The HRT also had limited access to shared information systems and
L1034@P38: could not conduct Coordinated Entry assessments – the entry point to access Alameda County
L1035@P38: shelter and resources – until September 2024, which hindered their ability to connect residents
L1036@P38-39: to services.
L1037@P39: ACTION CALENDAR
L1038@P39: Homeless Response Team: Opportunities Exist to Strengthen Procedures and Better Track Outcomes
L1039@P39: Pg. 2 of 2
L1040@P39: While the HRT tracked some outcomes related to its goals—such as shelter offers, encampment
L1041@P39: closures, and trash removal—it did not report on other meaningful outcomes like shelter
L1042@P39: enrollments or Coordinated Entry assessments until after the audit period. Reports were
L1043@P39: cumulative and not broken down by time period, which limited the ability to assess progress.
L1044@P39: Reports were also difficult to locate on the City’s website. HRT staff stated that limited
L1045@P39: administrative resources impacted their ability to analyze and report data.
L1046@P39: BACKGROUND
L1047@P39: The Berkeley City Council established the Homeless Response Team in 2021 to respond to
L1048@P39: encampments by conducting outreach and reducing health and safety threats without citation
L1049@P39: or arrest. Between 2022 and 2024, unsheltered homelessness in Berkeley decreased by 45
L1050@P39: percent—the largest decrease among the five largest cities in Alameda County. During this time,
L1051@P39: the City expanded its shelter and housing programs through local funding and state grants. The
L1052@P39: HRT is responsible for coordinating with other departments and providers but has limited
L1053@P39: authority over most shelter and housing placements. The team’s work is further shaped by legal
L1054@P39: constraints, including recent litigation and federal rulings on encampment actions. Local
L1055@P39: lawsuits, administrative regulations, and the City’s September 2024 Encampment Policy
L1056@P39: Resolution also affect how the HRT plans and conducts encampment interventions.
L1057@P39: ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY
L1058@P39: There are no identifiable environmental effects or opportunities associated with this report.
L1059@P39: RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
L1060@P39: The audit identified opportunities for the HRT to improve coordination with service providers,
L1061@P39: develop stronger procedures for internal data collection and reporting, and improve public
